paragraphs_reviewed_note: 27 sampled paragraphs (ch17: 0,1; ch18: 0,2,3,9,14; ch19: 0,5,7,10,12,13,22,23,27,28,29,31,36,38,39,40,41,42,43,47) plus the 4 flagged extras ch19 p6, p33, p34, p37. I also read all 15 ch18 paragraphs and most of the remaining ch19 paragraphs against the source, less closely. Nothing major turned up outside the sample.

findings.source_text: the power he hath till then usur
findings.candidate_text: the power he has until then usurped.
findings.problem: The Gutenberg source is cut off mid-word. The candidate completes it as 'usurped', which is the correct reading of §198. This should be logged in REVIEW-RECORD.md.
findings.suggested_fix: No text change. Log the truncation and the completion in REVIEW-RECORD.md.

findings.source_text: the anarchy being much alike, to have no form of government at all; ... Hence all commonwealths ... for the anarchy is much alike, to have no form of government at all
findings.candidate_text: The anarchy is much the same whether there is no form of government at all ... For the anarchy is much the same whether there is no form of government at all
findings.problem: I read the repetition as an editorial duplication, not Locke's own. I recall that in the corrected-copy text of §198 (Laslett) the clause appears once, and I think the 1764-derived text printed Locke's relocated clause in its new place without deleting it from the old one. The first occurrence has only 'design'; the second has 'know or design'. I am fairly but not fully confident of this. The candidate renders both faithfully to the served source, which is acceptable under the 1:1 rule, but a modern reader will see a word-for-word repeat as an error.
findings.suggested_fix: Acceptable as is if logged in REVIEW-RECORD.md. Better for a reading text, following the §2 precedent: drop the second sentence ('For the anarchy is much the same ... be the monarch.'), end the preceding sentence at 'settled methods of conveying the right to them.', and record this as a source correction.

findings.source_text: a point wherein a lawful king doth directly differ from a tyrant
findings.candidate_text: This is the point on which a lawful king directly differs from a tyrant.
findings.problem: James says 'a point'. The candidate's 'the point' anticipates, and slightly overstates, the next sentence's 'special and greatest point of difference'.
findings.suggested_fix: This is a point on which a lawful king directly differs from a tyrant.

findings.source_text: Hereafter, seed-time and harvest, ... shall not cease while the earth remaineth.
findings.candidate_text: ‘Hereafter, seed-time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night, shall not cease while the earth remaineth.’
findings.problem: None. The King James 1609 speech is modernized in full and in quotation marks. The Genesis 8:22 verse is kept verbatim, as the Scripture rule requires, and set in nested quotes. 'paction' becomes 'compact', 'deluge' becomes 'Flood' and 'leaves to be' becomes 'ceases to be', all correctly.

findings.source_text: if a long train of actions shew the councils all tending that way
findings.candidate_text: If a long train of actions shows that the councils are all tending that way
findings.problem: In 17th-century spelling 'councils' and 'counsels' were interchangeable, and Locke means the court's designs or plans. Modern 'councils' means advisory bodies, which misleads. Many modern editions print 'counsels' here.
findings.suggested_fix: If a long train of actions shows that the government's counsels [or: designs] are all tending that way

findings.source_text: as soon as the wind, weather, and other circumstances would let
findings.candidate_text: as soon as the wind, the weather and other circumstances would let him.
findings.problem: The source is cut off at the end of the chapter. The candidate completes it with 'let him', which is the standard reading, and 'let' there means 'allow', so it is correct modern usage. This should be logged in REVIEW-RECORD.md.

findings.source_text: An assembly of representatives chosen, pro tempore, by the people.
findings.candidate_text: An assembly of representatives chosen by the people for a limited term (pro tempore).
findings.problem: 'for a limited term' is the candidate's own gloss. The Latin policy keeps Latin untranslated, and the gloss over-specifies: pro tempore means 'for the time being', not a fixed term. It also moves the Latin out of Locke's word order. It should go.
findings.suggested_fix: An assembly of representatives chosen, pro tempore, by the people.  (If the editors want a gloss anyway, use 'chosen by the people pro tempore, that is, for the time being' and apply it consistently.)

findings.problem: The unintended pun 'still sit still' is awkward in modern prose.
findings.suggested_fix: and yet sit idle? / and yet do nothing?

findings.source_text: may, for aught I know, desire for his pains, a civil, respectful cudgeling
findings.candidate_text: may, for all I know, deserve for his pains a civil, respectful cudgelling
findings.problem: This is outside the sample. The candidate silently changes the source's 'desire' to 'deserve'. That is probably the right reading (standard editions print 'deserve'), but the style note requires suspected corruptions to be logged in REVIEW-RECORD.md, not silently corrected. REVIEW-RECORD.md does not exist yet.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep 'deserve' and log it as a source correction in REVIEW-RECORD.md. Otherwise revert to 'desire'.

findings.source_text: yet because he has hereby lost the principal part of regal dignity ... and also because he betrayed or forced his people ... By this, as it were, alienation of his kingdom, he himself loses the power
findings.candidate_text: yet he has thereby lost the principal part of royal dignity ...; and also, because he has betrayed or forced his people ..., by this alienation, as it were, of his kingdom he himself loses the power
findings.problem: Barclay gives two parallel reasons (because X, and because Y) for the forfeiture. The candidate drops the first 'because', so the loss of dignity becomes a bare statement and only the betrayal functions as a reason. The joined sentence is also hard to parse.
findings.suggested_fix: For though perhaps it may not be his intention to harm the people, yet he has thereby lost the principal part of royal dignity, namely, to be next and immediately under God, supreme in his kingdom; and he has also betrayed or forced his people, whose liberty he ought to have carefully preserved, into the power and dominion of a foreign nation. Because of both, by this alienation, as it were, of his kingdom he himself loses the power he had in it before, ...

findings.source_text: The mischief that is designed them, the people may prevent before it be done ... Such designs as these (says he) when any king harbours ... Because he betrayed or forced his people ... into the power and dominion of a foreign nation
findings.candidate_text: “The harm that is planned against them, the people may prevent before it is done” ... “When any king harbours such designs as these in his thoughts and seriously promotes them,” he says, “he immediately gives up all care and thought of the commonwealth.” ... “because he has betrayed or forced his people, whose liberty he ought to have carefully preserved.” ... “into the power and dominion of a foreign nation,”
findings.problem: None. I checked all four re-quotations character by character against the candidate's p29, p41 and p42 renderings, and they match exactly. Nothing from p43 is omitted (Bilson, Bracton, Fortescue, the Mirrour, Hooker and the Egyptian under-taskmasters are all present).
findings.suggested_fix: None. If p42 is revised per the finding above, keep the p43 quote 'because he has betrayed or forced his people, whose liberty he ought to have carefully preserved' in sync.

findings.source_text: Quod siquis dicat ... Barclay contra Monarchom. 1. iii. c. 8.
findings.problem: I checked programmatically that the Latin tail from 'Quod siquis' (1751 chars) is character-identical to the source, and so are p34 (129 chars), p37 (1525 chars) and p38 (818 chars). 'ubi tu pulsas, ego vapulo tantum' in p33 is also verbatim. The source Latin itself carries Gutenberg or print typos ('multitude' for multitudo, 'ulciscenti' for ulciscendi, 'resisit', 'meditator', 'amifit', and '1. iii.' for 'l. iii.'). The candidate keeps them verbatim, as the policy requires.
findings.suggested_fix: No change. Optionally list the Latin typos in REVIEW-RECORD.md.

findings.source_text: a great stickler for the power and prerogative of princes
findings.candidate_text: a great stickler for the power and prerogative of princes
findings.problem: This was the only hit in the archaism scan of ch17–19. 'stickler for' still carries Locke's sense ('zealous insister on') in modern English, so it is acceptable.

whole_chapter_scan: ch17–19 have zero hits for possessions, legislature, natural state/condition, state of warfare, hath, doth, whilst, wherein, whereby, thereof, shew, betwixt, viz., amongst, prejudice, mischief, aught or wherefore. 'possession' occurs only where Locke has it (ch17 p0, ch18 p11). Term counts match the source for consent, property/properties, legislative, state of war, state of nature, trust, prerogative, appeal to heaven, dissolution, commonwealth, estates, tyranny and rebel. There are two small differences: 'usurp' +2 (from the completed 'usurped' plus the helper wording in ch17 p0), and 'forfeit' +1 (ch19 p41, 'forfeits his dominion', which makes Locke's ellipsis explicit). Both are fine. 'rebellare' and 'rebellantes, rebels' are kept. ch19 p12 correctly drops the leaked label 'Sec. 219.'. Paragraph counts are 2/15/48, matching the source, and titles are unchanged.
summary: The rendering of ch17–19 is accurate and thorough. I found no omissions, reversals, dropped qualifications or term drift in the sampled paragraphs, and all Latin is character-identical to the source. The fixes are minor: 'councils' should read 'counsels' (ch18 p14), a slight overstatement in King James's 1603 speech (ch18 p2), the added 'for a limited term' gloss on pro tempore (ch19 p6), which should go, the lost parallel 'because' in Barclay's second case (ch19 p42), and 'still sit still' (ch19 p29). The two truncated source endings (ch17 'usur', ch18 'would let') are completed correctly. These completions, the silent 'desire' → 'deserve' change in ch19 p35, and the ch17 p1 duplicated anarchy clause (in my judgement an editorial duplication rather than Locke's own repetition) all need entries in REVIEW-RECORD.md, which does not yet exist.
